planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in full sun to light shade in fertile, well-drained soil, sheltered from harsh winter wind.

directions: Grow willow-leaf bay in full sun to light shade in fertile, well-drained soil, sheltered from harsh winter wind in the colder part of its range. This RHS Award of Garden Merit form of common bay is prized for slender, willow-like leaves with a gently undulating edge that give the whole shrub a finer, more feathery texture than plain bay laurel. New leaves emerge with a coppery flush before settling into deep matte green, and small clusters of pale yellow-green flowers appear along the stems in spring. The narrow leaves are just as pungent as the species and can be picked and dried for the kitchen at any time once the plant is established; clip lightly through the growing season to maintain a dense, formal shape or leave it looser as a specimen tree.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Laurus nobilis f. angustifolia
International Dendrology Society — Trees and Shrubs Online
North Carolina State Extension — Laurus nobilis

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in a sheltered, frost-free site with humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil.

directions: Plant Azores laurel in humus-rich, reliably moist, well-drained soil in a sheltered site with full sun to partial shade, choosing the warmest microclimate available since it is noticeably less cold-hardy than Mediterranean bay laurel. Endemic to the Azores and Canary Islands, this Macaronesian laurel-forest tree forms one of the dominant canopy species of the ancient til woodlands and can eventually reach substantial size, with downy young twigs and much larger leaves than common bay laurel. Crushed foliage releases the same warm, aromatic bay fragrance and has traditionally been used interchangeably with Laurus nobilis in regional cooking, though in cultivation outside its native range it is grown mainly as a rare specimen tree for large gardens and conservatories in mild climates. Because it is dioecious, only female trees produce the small blue-black fruit that follows the pale greenish-yellow spring flowers; site young plants away from cold, exposed positions and mulch well to conserve soil moisture.
sources: International Dendrology Society — Trees and Shrubs Online
Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil; give it room, since roots are vigorous and spreading.

directions: Site 'Crispa' in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil; once established it needs little supplemental water and tolerates the same dry-summer conditions as the species. This dense, pyramidal cultivar is grown for its tightly undulating, crimped leaf margins — the wavy 'pie crust' edge is most pronounced on container-grown plants and gives the foliage a distinctive ruffled texture that stands out in wreaths and holiday arrangements. Small inconspicuous yellow flowers appear in spring, and the aromatic leaves can be harvested and used in the kitchen exactly like ordinary bay laurel. Give it room to grow, since it is a vigorous, fast-growing selection with an assertive root system best kept away from foundations or hardscaping, and protect container specimens when temperatures drop much below 12°F.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to part shade in ordinary, well-drained soil; water regularly the first two years, then only during dry spells.

directions: Plant Saratoga bay laurel in full sun to part shade in ordinary, well-drained soil; it tolerates lean or poor soil and, once established after about two years, needs only infrequent irrigation. This compact, naturally tidy selection of common bay laurel produces glossy, rounded, olive-green leaves that emerge with a reddish blush, along with small pale yellow flowers in late winter and early spring; because it is a male selection it never sets the messy black fruit of seed-grown bay laurel. It shows better resistance to laurel psyllid and soft scale than the species and is popular trained as a clipped standard, multi-trunk patio tree, or clean, low-litter hedge. Left unpruned it can reach 20 to 25 feet, but it responds well to shaping and is equally at home sheared tight or grown loose as a specimen.
sources: UC Master Gardener Program of Sonoma County
